Thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Moldova.

Mr. President, Excellencies, colleagues, the Republic of Moldova aligns itself to the statement delivered by the European Union and would like to make the following remarks in its national capacity. Mr. President, Russia's illegal, unjustified and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine continues to cause immense human suffering and undermine the principles of the United Nations Charter. For more than four years, civilians have been killed and injured, families uprooted and critical infrastructure destroyed. In the temporarily occupied territories, people continue to face repression and grave human rights violations. We remain deeply concerned about reports of unlawful detention, torture, enforced disappearances, conflict-related sexual violence, forced displacement and the deportation and unlawful transfer of Ukrainian children. All alleged violations of international law must be independently investigated and those responsible held accountable. The Republic of Moldova does not recognize and will not recognize any change in the status of Ukraine's territories resulting from Russian aggression. So-called elections, referendums, and other attempts to legitimize occupation have no validity under international law. They violate the United Nations Charter, the Helsinki Final Act, and the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. We reaffirm our unwavering support for Ukraine's sovereign territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, commend the courage of its people in defending their freedom, and call on the Russian Federation to cease its aggression and withdraw all its forces from Ukraine. Since the beginning of the full scale invasion, the Moldovan authorities have provided political, diplomatic and humanitarian support to Ukraine. The Republic of Moldova remains a reliable partner to Ukraine, including by offering the assistance to the displaced Ukrainian citizens, strengthening regional connectivity, facilitating transit of essential goods, contributing to Ukraine's energy resilience. We are committed to continuing our support to Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. Mr. President, Russia's aggression has also directly affected the Republic of Moldova. Russian drones have repeatedly violated our sovereign airspace, while attacks against Ukraine's energy infrastructure have disrupted essential services and endangered our citizens. Our country has also confronted with disinformation, cyber attacks, electoral interference and energy blackmail aimed at destabilizing our society. These threats show that Moldova's security and Ukrainian security are inseparable. Stronger Ukrainian defense also means safer skies for Moldova and greater regional security. Excellencies, the Republic of Moldova supports all genuine efforts to achieve a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace consistent with the UN Charter, international law, and relevant General Assembly resolutions. A ceasefire must neither legitimize territorial conquest nor freeze the consequences of aggression. It must lead to the restoration of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity and be supported by credible security guarantees. There can be no durable peace without justice. The Republic of Moldova therefore supports international efforts to ensure accountability for all crimes committed in connection with Russia's aggression. We are proud to be among the founding members of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine within the framework of the Council of Europe. Together with the Register of Damage and the International Claims Commission for Ukraine, this represents an essential step forward towards justice and reparation for the victims. Mr. President, this war concerns wherever borders may be changed through force, occupation normalized, and sovereignty of smaller states disregarded. The answer of this assembly must remain clear. Aggression cannot be rewarded, occupation cannot be recognized, and peace cannot be built at the expense of the victim. The people of the Republic of Moldova stands with the people of Ukraine. Ukraine's independence strengthens our independence, its security strengthens our security. And a just peace for Ukraine will strengthen the rules-based international order upon which we all depend. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Republic of Moldova. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Mr. President, at the outset, I would like to thank you for convening this crucial meeting today. We recognize and appreciate the presence of Deputy Foreign Minister Marianna Bedza today with us and her informative, if sobering, statement. Poland aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the European Union, and I would like to add the following remarks in my national capacity. Mr. President, years pass, and yet we find ourselves in the same position, continuously appalled by Russia's illegal and coercive actions committed in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine since 2014. Forced Russification, deportation, restrictions on fundamental freedoms, militarization, and indoctrination of Ukrainian children, as well as severe mistreatment of detainees and prisoners of war are just a few examples of Russia's policy implemented in Ukraine, policy aimed at shattering lives, rights, and identity of those living under occupation. According to the latest UN findings, more than 92% of civilians reported torture or ill treatment, or 30% referred to as acts of sexual violence. Thanks to the efforts of the OHCHR, we also know that displacement and property confiscation reinforce one another. People flee because of threats of fear of detention, but upon return, they may find their homes declared abandoned and confiscated by the occupier. In Donetsk and Luhansk alone, the UN has documented at least 5,600 private properties registered as abandoned. Equally troubling, yet not surprising, is Russia's human resources policy at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, where staff have experienced retaliation after refusing to sign contracts with Rosatom, a stark illustration of how human rights violations can put nuclear safety at risk. Even facts and figures are helpless when faced with Russia's inhumane policy towards the children. Transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children continue, just as denying access to education in Ukrainian language, and subjecting children to the so-called patriotic and military education, which is nothing more than yet another effort to erase their national identity. This must end. We welcome the conclusion of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry, according to which the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children by Russian authorities constitute crimes against humanity as well as war crimes. We hope that every state present in this room today shares this view, not out of political correctness, but out of respect for the facts. Against this backdrop, accountability must remain at the center of our response. Russia's international crimes must be investigated and prosecuted, and victims must be granted access to justice and effective remedies. Even though the recent scale of Russian attacks proves that Moscow is unwilling to end its hostilities against Ukraine, we call on Russia for the hundredth time to stop its illegal and aggressive actions and to ensure unfettered access for independent international monitors to all temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. Mr. President, in conclusion, let me state clearly, Russia's provocative posture in the region and recent violations of airspace of Poland, Romania, Republic of Moldova, and Latvia by missiles and drones do not bring us close to ending the conflict. Perhaps a novelty for Russia, a country with actual neo-colonial ambitions, But undermining security architecture does not help restore peace. Complete and unconditional withdrawal from the illegally occupied territories does. Crimea, Sevastopol, Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia are Ukraine. We will not turn a blind eye to the atrocities committed by Moscow in Ukraine. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkey.

Mr. President, let me start by thanking Your Excellency for convening this debate on the situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as the war in Ukraine continues to have profound global implications for international peace and security. Let me reiterate Turkey's principal position. Turkey has been supporting Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence since the occupation and illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014. Turkey maintains its firm stance of not recognizing the de facto situation. This position is not a matter of political preference. It is rooted in our commitment to the principles of the UN charter and international law, which remain critical in preserving the credibility of the multilateral system. Given our shared history, the well-being of the Crimean Tatars, our kinsmen, the preservation of their identity, culture, language and rights, and their ability to safety and dignity in their homeland are a matter of profound importance to Turkey. Crimean Tatars' heritage in the region should be safeguarded. We will continue to support Crimean Tatars with a view to preserving their identity and ensuring that they live in their historical homeland in peace and security. We are equally concerned about the broader human rights situation in the temporarily occupied territories and remain deeply concerned with the human cost of the war across Ukraine. Mr. President, behind every statistic stands a human life. That's why, since the outset, Turkey has consistently advocated for a negotiated settlement in Ukraine and proactively engaged in diplomatic efforts. It was Turkey who brought together the warring sides around the negotiating table in 2022 and '25. The Black Sea Grain Initiative demonstrated that concrete arrangements could be achieved even in the midst of a raging war when there is sufficient political will and effective mediation. Last year, the three rounds of talks hosted in Istanbul yielded concrete progress, particularly in addressing urgent humanitarian concerns between the parties, including exchange of prisoners of war in substantial numbers. As the first direct encounter between the parties after years, the talks served as an important confidence-building measure. Currently, as the stalemate in the diplomatic process grinds on, we are alarmed by the escalation in war, causing many civilian losses and material damage. Civilians have suffered far too long. They deserve peace. Therefore, it is essential to revitalize the negotiation process between Russia and Ukraine. In that, the UN has a greater role to play. We must consistently uphold the principles of the UN Charter while ensuring that the organization remains capable of facilitating dialogue rather than becoming merely a platform for exchanging accusations. Furthermore, developments in the Black Sea pose an urgent and visible threat to the security of the wider region. Black Sea has a strategic importance for supplying grain and agricultural products to world markets. The reciprocal attacks in the maritime domain And disruption of sea trade leave countries in the global south vulnerable to rising food prices, once again demonstrating the far-reaching devastating consequences of the war. Mr. President, peace will require difficult compromises. It will require addressing thorny issues of security and legitimacy. But above all, it requires political courage. Yet, we are hopeful that further rounds of talks between Russia and Ukraine may build a renewed momentum which will eventually pave the way to peace. We will continue to work for an end to this war through diplomacy. Turkey remains committed to achieving a just and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the principles of international law and the UN Charter. Thank you again.
I thank the distinguished representative of Turkey. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Austria.

Mr. President, Excellencies, colleagues, last week Ukraine marked 35 years of independence. Austria congratulates the Ukrainian people. In 1991, more than 90% of Ukrainians voted for independence, with a majority in every region, including Crimea.

Russia recognized Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and borders shortly afterwards. Yet today, Russia's actions stand in direct contradiction to these commitments.

As a military neutral country, Austria does not supply weapons.

Our support is humanitarian and political.

Close to 100,000 Ukrainians.

Have found refuge in Austria, and Austria has provided close to $400 million in bilateral financial and humanitarian assistance, in.

Addition to its contribution through European Union budget and instruments. Three points are central to Austria's position. First, international law and the UN Charter must remain our guiding stars.

Austria rejects the tenet that illegal occupation and the violation of any country's sovereignty are legitimate means of pursuing politics.

No.

Country in the world should have to accept facts that are established by military means in contravention of the charter. Second, the occupation and the wider war have horrible consequences for civilians. In occupied territory, UN reports, in particular by the OHCHR and Commission of Inquiry.

Document arbitrary detention, torture, and forced conscription.

Civilians unlawfully transferred or deported, including children, must be returned, and international monitors must be granted access.

Attacks against civilians and civilian objects, as well as indiscriminate attacks, violate international humanitarian.

Law, which must be respected by all at all times.

Third, the immediate priority is to stop the fighting. Austria calls for a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire.

It should open the way to negotiations between the parties on a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace based on the UN charter and international law. Austria is ready to offer its good offices.

And host talks in Vienna on the war in Ukraine and the broader question of the European security architecture.

The United Nations and the OSCE, both with headquarters in Vienna.

Could play an important role in the implementation of a ceasefire or a broader peace agreement. In addition, we need to recall the humanitarian effects of the war extend far beyond Ukraine. Attacks on Black Sea ports and commercial vessels disrupt agricultural exports, raising food prices worldwide. The effects are greatest in countries least able to absorb them. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Austria. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Denmark.

Mr. President, Denmark aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union and by Finland on behalf of the Nordic Baltic states. One week ago, Ukraine celebrated the 35th anniversary of regaining its independence. This was an independence hard fought and hard won. It was and remains an internationally recognized independence with internationally recognized borders and protections. Today, however, and for more than 12 years, those borders and protections have come under direct assault from the Russian Federation. For 12 years, in clear violations of the UN Charter, Russia has attempted to redraw Ukraine's borders by force, to erase Ukraine from the map, subjugate the Ukrainian people, and deny them their right to choose their own future. And for 12 years, Russia has failed. Mr. President, today's debate is a vital opportunity to send a strong and united message to the estimated 3.5 million Ukrainians trapped in the Russian temporarily occupied territories. A message of solidarity and of support. A reminder that the international community stands with them and has not forgotten them. Russia has long prevented independent observers, including UN bodies, from entering these territories. However, the testimonies of those who have managed to escape shine a light on what life under Russian occupation has become. It is a life where the most vulnerable, often children, suffer the most, where schools are used to reinforce political control and indoctrination, where the Ukrainian language is effectively banned and a Russian passport is required to graduate, where propaganda is relentless and military training for a foreign army is mandatory. This is the reality for hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian children in the temporarily occupied territories. And many thousands more, however, have been unlawfully deported and forcibly transferred to Russia itself. In this regard, Denmark demands that Russia fully complies with last year's General Assembly resolution demanding the immediate, safe and unconditional return of these children. Similarly, Ukrainian adults are also subjected to attempts to eradicate their identity. A Russian passport is needed to access all basic services. Ukrainians who refuse Russian citizenship risk deportation to Russia. Outward displays of Ukrainian identity and culture have become dangerous, with civilians regularly detained on false charges and subjected to arbitrary imprisonment and severe abuse. Political detainees are sent to penal colonies across the border in Russia. And as the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission has assessed, Ukrainians detained by Russia are subject to widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment, including physical abuse, psychological terror, and sexual violence. Mr. President, the reported conditions Ukrainian experience in the occupied territories clearly violate international humanitarian law. Denmark condemns all violations of international humanitarian law in the strongest terms. Russia's illegal invasions of Ukraine have not led to peace, not in 2014, not in 2022, and not today. Denmark calls on Russia to immediately halt its illegal war of aggression and to accept Ukraine's offer of an unconditional, immediate and comprehensive ceasefire. This is the essential first step to a just and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Denmark. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece.

Only last week, we commemorated the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence, an independence explicitly recognised yet flagrantly violated by the Russian Federation. Russia attacked an illegally occupied sovereign territory of Ukraine in blatant violation of international law and the UN Charter. In Crimea, Sevastopol, Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, Ukrainians are daily deprived of their human rights and fundamental freedoms. Russian attacks on Ukraine continue unabated. Since the beginning of the war, more than 16,000 civilians have been killed, including 820 children. Russian strikes increasingly target densely populated urban centers far from the front line, while long-range weapons, drones, and aerial bombardments continue to inflict a devastating toll on civilians. We condemn all attacks against civilians and critical infrastructure as a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and call for their immediate cessation. We also call upon Russia to ensure full, safe, and unhindered humanitarian access in the illegally occupied territories of Ukraine. The human rights situation is equally alarming. Restrictions on freedom of expression, religion, and Ukrainian language education, coupled with arbitrary detentions, form part of the grim reality faced by Ukrainians daily. Politically motivated persecutions, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment, sexual violence, and forcible transfer of civilians, especially children, complete this bleak picture. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine and the UN Commission of Inquiry have been unequivocal in documenting these grave violations. Greece strongly condemns these violations and calls for thorough investigations and full accountability. We call upon Russia to grant international monitoring mechanism full access to the temporarily occupied territories. We further support the exchange of all prisoners of war and the release of all persons arbitrarily detained. We also reiterate our demand for the immediate return of all unlawfully deported or transferred Ukrainian children. The repercussions of the war extend far beyond Ukraine. Attacks against vessels and seaport infrastructure in the Black Sea threaten maritime security, global food security, and international trade. Greece reiterates that freedom of navigation must be fully protected in accordance with international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. For our part, we remain committed to safeguarding maritime food supply chains through our commercial shipping fleet, as we all have done consistently in the past, provided that a secure, predictable operational environment is guaranteed. Colleagues, Russia must end its hostilities and return to the negotiating table. We reiterate our call for a full ceasefire as a first step towards meaningful negotiations aimed at achieving a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law, the UN Charter and the General Assembly resolutions. We reaffirm our unwavering solidarity and support for the Ukrainian people. Greece remains committed to the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders and rejects any attempt to alter borders by force. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Greece. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you very much, Mr President. Since the beginning of this conflict, Mexico has expressed its profound concern at its consequences. Our position stands firm and unchanged. International law cannot be applied selectively and the UN Charter should be respected in its entirety in all cases. International law also demands the effective protection of the civilian population and of humanitarian personnel in any conflict setting. This is particularly relevant in occupied territories. We recall that occupation does not grant sovereignty over an occupied territory nor does it exempt the occupying power from its international obligations. The reality remains catastrophic. Densely populated areas have suffered recurrent attacks that have caused serious damage to homes, schools, hospitals, and cultural sites. According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, between January and July this year, the fighting killed 1,839 people and wounded another 10,638. This is a 44% rise when compared with the same period in 2025 and more than double the number of the victims in 2024. This is compounded by the worsening conditions for humanitarian assistance. This year so far in Ukraine, at least 10 humanitarian workers have died and 39 have been wounded. Behind these figures are lives cut short, families displaced and entire communities suffering a protracted war. We must not overlook the overwhelming need to address the impact of the conflict on the mental health and well being of women and children who have suffered mental trauma related to the direct experience of physical and sexual violence. Mexico notes with concern the repercussions of arms transfers in this conflict that heighten the risks for weapons diversion, indiscriminate use and the loss of control over those weapons. We condemn the use of explosive arms in densely populated areas and we reject the use of weapons that are banned under international law such as cluster munitions and anti-personnel mines due to their indiscriminate and harmful effects on the civilian population. We unequivocally condemn, we need to also be emphatic that any attacks on nuclear facilities must be brought to an end. Mr President, the end of this war shouldn't be measured by the military capacity of the parties, but rather by the determination and commitment to make diplomacy the instrument for a negotiated, lasting and acceptable solution for both sides. We value the various proposals, peace proposals made by the other countries. As a member of the Group of Friends for Peace in Ukraine, Mexico remains committed to building bridges of dialogue between the various actors to establishing an enabling environment for any peace negotiation. Mexico reiterates the importance for the UN to play an active role and to serve as the guarantor for any peace agreement with the participation of the parties involved. We underscore that peace should address the needs and aspirations of the population while also preserving the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine in accordance with international law. We cannot allow the prolonged conflict to make civilian suffering, the destruction of infrastructure, and nuclear risk a new normality. Our responsibility is to enforce one of the most emblematic sentences in the UN Charter's preamble, which is to preserve succeeding generations from war. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Mr. President, Slovenia aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the European Union. Russia's illegal occupation of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol began in 2014. Since then, Russia has expanded its illegal occupation to parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 marked a dramatic escalation of its aggression. This war of aggression constitutes a blatant breach of the core principles of the United Nations charter. It violates Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. Slovenia has been clear on this from the beginning. Crimea and Sevastopol, as well as Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions are part of Ukraine. Internationally recognized borders cannot be changed by force. Against this background, Slovenia is deeply concerned by the sharp rise in civilian casualties. Recent UN reporting shows that the human cost of Russia's aggression continues to grow. We condemn attacks against civilians and civilian objects, as well as indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks in the strongest possible terms. International humanitarian law must be respected at all times. Mr. President, children require our particular attention. Slovenia strongly condemns the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children by Russian authorities to Russian territory or to areas they occupied in Ukraine. The Independent International Commission of Inquiry in Ukraine has found that such acts in the situation it examined amount to war crimes. Thousands of Ukrainian children have been deprived of their liberty, subjected to alternation of their identity, indoctrination, and even adoptions, and have suffered from trauma and anxiety. These practices must end. Slovenia calls upon Russia to ensure the immediate, safe, and unconditional return of all unlawfully deported and forcibly transferred Ukrainian children to Ukraine. The protection of children in strict compliance with international humanitarian law and international human rights law must remain a priority. Mr. President, there must be accountability for these violations. A just peace cannot be built on impunity. Slovenia reaffirms our support for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, grounded in international law and the UN Charter, including respect for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Russia must end its violations of international law. It must end its illegal occupation of Ukrainian territory and respect the rights and dignity of the people living under occupation. It must cease its war of aggression against Ukraine. A just and lasting peace must be based on the UN Charter, international law, and full respect for Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Croatia.

Thank you, President. Croatia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, and I wish to add some remarks in my national capacity. Mr. President, in July, the High Commissioner for Human Rights reported that civilian casualties in Ukraine increased by an appalling 40% during the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year. intensified targeted attacks on populated areas, as well as the large-scale use of drones along the front lines, are taking a heavy toll on the civilian population, which has already been suffering for years. At the same time, limited access to information from occupied territories means that its true scale is likely considerably higher. In addition, reports from these territories continue to reveal a persistent pattern of violence and serious human rights violations by the Russian Federation. Freedoms are severely restricted. Protected persons are forcibly conscripted into Russian armed forces, and children are denied access to Ukrainian education. The treatment of detainees is particularly alarming. Ukrainian civilians continue to be detained in occupied territories or transferred to detention facilities in Russia. More than 95% of released Ukrainian prisoners of war registered by OHCHR reported torture or ill treatment. OHCHR has also documented executions of prisoners of war and deaths in custody, including as a result from torture, denial of medical care, and inhumane detention conditions. These findings further confirm that Russia's war of aggression continues to be marked by grave violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. Mr. President, Croatia strongly supports diplomatic efforts aimed at ending Russia's aggression against Ukraine and achieving a just and sustainable peace as soon as possible. Meaningful diplomacy pursued in good faith and with clarity of purpose is indispensable. But a ceasefire alone cannot provide lasting peace. It must be part of a comprehensive settlement firmly grounded in the UN Charter and international law. Based on its own experience of imposed war and occupation all the way to the full territorial reintegration, including by peaceful and diplomatic means, Croatia can attest that durable peace requires patience and perseverance, respect for fundamental principles, justice, and accountability. borders cannot be changed by force and aggression must not be rewarded with territory even in times of armed conflict civilian population as well as prisoners of war must be protected and human rights fully respected Croatia therefore remains firmly committed to Ukraine's sovereignty independence and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders and will continue to stand in solidarity with Ukraine and its people I thank you
I thank the distinguished representative of Croatia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Mr. President, four years on, the conflict in Ukraine has taken a devastating human toll and yielded far-reaching consequences for international peace and security. Today, the conclusion is crystal clear: a resolution to this conflict will not be found in the military domain. Further escalation will only bring more destruction and death, deepen mistrust and hatred, and make the path towards peace ever more difficult. Brazil reiterates its call for deescalation and for an immediate and comprehensive ceasefire. All efforts should be directed at creating conditions for meaningful negotiations. Only diplomacy can bring a just and lasting peace. in accordance with our charter and considering the legitimate security concerns of the parties involved. But while diplomacy understandably takes time, human suffering must cease without any further delay. The human consequences of this conflict have been devastating. International humanitarian law applies to all parties at all times without exception. Civilians and civilian objects must be protected. Attacks against homes, hospitals, energy systems, and other infrastructure indispensable to civilian life must stop immediately. The principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution must be strictly and unconditionally observed. Military operations involving or conducted in the vicinity of nuclear installations may have consequences that could extend far beyond the battlefield. Such facilities must never become targets of military operations. Brazil is particularly concerned by the extensive use of unmanned aerial systems in the conflict and their negative humanitarian impact. Regardless of the technology employed, all parties must fully respect international humanitarian law by ensuring meaningful human control over weapons systems employed in the conflict. In 2025, global military spending exceeded $2.8 trillion, a 41% increase over the past decade, and at least 16 times the amount of international development assistance. Every dollar spent on armaments is a dollar not spent on fighting hunger, poverty, inequality, and climate change. Every additional day of this war increases the human, economic, and political cost of peace. We should not resign into managing an indefinite protracted conflict. Our collective responsibility is to help bring it to an end. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

Mr President, I would like to begin by welcoming the participation here of the Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, Marianna Betza. To complement the EU statement on behalf of the Member States, I would like to add the following. Thirty-five years ago, the Ukrainian parliament proclaimed the independence of the country. This was a choice that was confirmed a few months later by a referendum that garnered 92% favorable votes for the nationality across all of the regions of the country. The independence of Ukraine and the tracing of its borders were then recognized by the international community, including Russia, which committed at the time to respect them. Contravening these bilateral commitments and flouting the United Nations Charter, Russia in 2014 called into question the territorial integrity of Ukraine by by illegally annexing Crimea and the city of Sevastopol. In 2014, the General Assembly already denounced the sham referendum organised at the time and decided that it was not valid, it could not serve as a basis for any modification to the status. After in 2022 launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia illegally annexed four additional regions of Ukraine, Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhia. In October 2022, almost four years ago, this Assembly also condemned this attempted illegal annexation. This also carried out through a sham referendum. Mr President, France roundly condemns the policies conducted by Russia in the occupied Ukrainian territories. The report of the High Commissioner for Human Rights reports grave violations, repeated persistent violations, be they displacement, forced deportation, arbitrary detention, acts of torture and treatment in detention, but also violations of the rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of expression and freedom of religion. France also wishes to express its profound concern with regard to the documented measures to impose Russian citizenship, to expropriate goods, to restrict the expressions of Ukrainian citizenship. These are unacceptable and profoundly affect the ability of the population to live freely and to preserve its identity. Such practices are part of a determination to to that has no legal validity. We reaffirm our support for the international mechanisms to establish the facts and to combat impunity. The protection of human rights must remain at the heart of our collective action. No peace, can be lasting if it is founded while undermining human dignity and no grave violation should go unresponded. Every day of the escalation is ever more deadly. carried out by Moscow against the civilian population and vital infrastructure. We call on Russia to seriously respond to the offers of mediation made. It falls solely to Russia to accept a ceasefire demanded by the vast majority of UN Member States. Mr President, France and its partners will continue to work for a peaceful settlement of the dispute. We will continue to provide Ukraine with the support that it needs to defend its sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of France. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies. Germany aligns itself with a statement delivered by the European Union. We meet today to address the ongoing and severe human rights crisis unfolding across the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. In more than four years of Russia's ongoing war of aggression, we have witnessed the most egregious violations of human rights and of international law. And please allow me to highlight three areas of particular concern. First, we are gravely concerned about the treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war and unlawfully detained civilians captivated by Russia. The findings of UN human rights monitoring missions are deeply disturbing. They document widespread and systematic torture and ill treatment of prisoners of war and civilians in Russian captivity. We reiterate the call for unhindered, immediate and regular access by the International Committee of the Red Cross and other independent human rights mechanisms. We call on the Russian Federation to immediately end all torture and ill-treatment and to ensure adequate detention conditions and medical care. Second, Germany remains deeply alarmed by the systematic violence against children. The ongoing listing of Russian armed forces and affiliated groups for grave violations against children, including the killing and maiming of children and attacks on protected civilian objects such as schools and hospitals, underscores Russia's blatant disregard for international laws protecting children

in war zones.

The unlawful deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children is a gross violation of international law and amounts to crimes against humanity. We utterly condemn these acts. The systematic separation of children from their families, the forcible alteration of their personal status, citizenship and identity, and efforts to obstruct their repatriation are unbearable.

They demand a unified response.

The Secretary-General's annual report on children and armed conflict, the Office of the High Commissioner and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe have all verified and documented the appalling scale of abduction and forced transfer of Ukrainian children by the Russian authorities. We reiterate our unwavering call for the immediate safe and unconditional return of all abducted Ukrainian children to their families or legal guardians. Third, we strongly condemn Russia's use of sexual violence as a weapon of war, torture and repression. Sexual violence has been used to terrorize and humiliate, to punish and intimidate Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war, forming a systematic pattern of violence and repression by Russia. We welcome the Secretary-General's decision in this year's annual report on conflict-related sexual violence to list the Russian armed and security forces. These violations must stop. Survivors must have unhindered and immediate access to comprehensive medical and psychosocial support and justice, and perpetrators must be held accountable. Germany actively supports international accountability and justice for crimes committed during Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine through legal, financial, and investigative assistance. To this end, we support the establishment of an international claims commission and the special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine. We also support the investigations by the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, both financially and by seconding experts. Mr. President, excellencies, Germany stands with the people of Ukraine. We reaffirm our support for Ukrainian independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. And we are committed to pursue accountability for Russia's consistent violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. I thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Peace lies at the core of the United Nations mandate. Yet across the world, conflicts endure, divisions widen, and the prospect of peace remains distant. Ukraine has now endured more than three years of war, with continuing loss of life, human suffering, and destruction. Its consequences are also being felt well beyond the battlefield. The international community continues to expect the United Nations to help chart a path toward peace. We must therefore maintain a firm, consistent, and collective message to all parties. First, end the hostilities and secure a durable ceasefire. Let us continue to make a clear and unified call for an end to hostilities. This is indispensable to creating the conditions for meaningful peace talks. Only then can genuine space for diplomacy and meaningful negotiations emerge. Second, uphold the UN Charter and international law. Lasting peace can only be built on respect for international law, including international humanitarian law. Civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected at all times. Humanitarian assistance must reach all those in need safely and without impediment. Indonesia has contributed concretely to Ukraine's recovery. We have supported the reconstruction of medical facilities in Ukraine, reflecting our commitment to tangible humanitarian action. Furthermore, we underscore the urgency of international cooperation to enhance capacity to deliver humanitarian aid. Third, intensify efforts toward dialogue and a peaceful settlement. Indonesia remains convinced that dialogue is the only viable path out of this prolonged conflict. We must never relent Let me repeat, we must never relent in our efforts to pursue this goal. The international community must help create the conditions necessary for the resumption of meaningful negotiations. Indonesia underscores the vital role of the United Nations, particularly the General Assembly, the Security Councils, in advancing multilateralism, fostering dialogue and promoting peace, including through the peaceful, safe and responsible use of emerging technologies. Hence, we should also support credible peace initiatives that address the underlying causes of the conflict. This is in line with our collective efforts to further invest in peace and enhance mediation. Mr. President, Indonesia stresses that the pursuit of peace must be consistent and free from double standards, whether in Ukraine, Gaza, or elsewhere. Humanity must prevail over politics interests. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Georgia.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, Georgia aligns with the statement delivered by the European Union, and I would

like to deliver the following remarks in my national capacity. At the outset, let me highlight the importance of maintaining the General Assembly's close

attention to the situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine as

Russia's ongoing aggression continues to pose a grave challenge to international peace and security and to the fundamental principles of international order. We reiterate Georgia's unwavering support for the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders and territorial waters. We remain firmly committed to the principle that internationally recognized borders cannot be altered through the use of or threat of force. We are also deeply concerned by the continued reports of serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine and in areas under the control of Russian Federation. Reports of torture and ill treatment, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, conflict-related sexual violence, Summary executions and other grave violations demand the continued attention of the international community. International humanitarian law must always be respected. Distinguished delegates, Georgia knows firsthand the long-term human cost of illegal occupation. For more than three decades, Russia's illegal occupation of Georgia's Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions has continued to affect the security,

human rights, and humanitarian situation on the ground.

International monitoring mechanisms continue to face restrictions to access these regions, while conflict-affected populations continue to face serious challenges.

This experience has reinforced Georgia's conviction that sustained international engagement, independent monitoring and accountability are indispensable for protecting human rights and preventing the normalization of occupation.

enshrined in the UN Charter and Helsinki Final Act.

and uphold international law.

Thank you, President. For over 135 years, the IPU has worked for peace through multilateralism and parliamentary diplomacy. The IPU was founded on the belief that lasting peace begins when representatives of nations, friends and foes, meet, listen and try to find solutions. when words are exchanged instead of bullets. In its resolution and multiple pronouncement, the IPU has strongly reaffirmed the principles at the heart of international law, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the prohibition of the use and threat of force to resolve disputes. These pillars are a system designed to protect.

Us all.

And when these pillars are flouted and ignored, international relations become unstable, unpredictable and dangerous. The war in Ukraine has torn apart communities, cost countless lives and forced millions from their homes.

It has shaken.

To the core, the very order that had preserved peace in Europe sees the end of the Cold War. The IPU has spoken clearly. From the outset, the IPU has called for the urgent need to bring about a ceasefire, secure human corridors, a return to diplomacy. It has condemned Russia's military aggression against Ukraine, as well as the unlawful annexation of its territories. The IPU Task Force on the peaceful resolution of the war in Ukraine, established in the spring of 2022, took this principle to heart. It has opened parliamentary discussion with both Ukrainian and the Russian Federation on nuclear safety, food security, environmental harm, the treatment of prisoners, and the tragic fate of displaced and abducted Ukrainian children. These exchanges are modest steps, but they keep the path to dialogue open and lay the groundwork for peace tomorrow, a just and lasting peace uncovered in the fundamental principle of international law. Delegates, peace is more than the end of violence. It's not achieved simply when guns fall silent. True peace demands a foundation built on human security, on societies where every individual can live in dignity, free from fear and injustice, and on community that give each person the chance to thrive. Lasting peace rests on a simple truth. No nation can be secure in isolation. Peace is not an abstract goal, but a daily effort, an act of solidarity of empathy and of political courage. On behalf of the IPU, I encourage all of us here to commit to working for peace in Ukraine now.
